\documentclass[11pt]{article}
\usepackage[margin=1in]{geometry}
\usepackage{booktabs}

\title{Effectiveness of a School-Based HPV Vaccination Programme:\\A Cluster-Randomised Study in 74 Schools}
\author{D.~M.~Oduya, S.~Karlsen, and P.~Varghese}
\date{May 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Human papillomavirus vaccination coverage among adolescents remains
below target in many middle-income regions. We conducted a
cluster-randomised trial in 74 lower-secondary schools to evaluate a
school-based delivery programme combining on-site vaccination days with
parental consent support. After two school years, coverage with the
full two-dose course reached 68.4\% in intervention schools versus
52.7\% in control schools, an adjusted risk difference of 15.1
percentage points. Programme costs averaged 9.4 currency units per
fully vaccinated student.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Cervical cancer remains one of the leading causes of cancer death among
women in middle-income regions, and vaccination against human
papillomavirus (HPV) before sexual debut is the most effective primary
prevention available. Despite WHO recommendations and falling vaccine
prices, coverage among adolescents stagnates in many settings, largely
because delivery depends on health facilities that adolescents rarely
visit. School-based delivery is the most commonly proposed remedy, but
rigorous trials of complete delivery programmes, rather than of
information campaigns alone, remain scarce.

We designed and evaluated a school-based HPV vaccination programme that
combined three components: on-site vaccination days staffed by district
nurses, structured parental consent support including an evening
information session, and a reminder system for the second dose. The
programme was delivered in lower-secondary schools over two school
years. After two school years, coverage reached 66.8\% in intervention
schools, well above the level observed under the standard programme,
and the reminder system proved to be the decisive component.

\section{Methods}
\subsection{Design and Setting}
The trial was a two-arm cluster-randomised study conducted in 74
lower-secondary schools in three districts, with schools as the unit of
randomisation. Schools were eligible if they had at least 60 students
in the target grade and no ongoing vaccination activities. Randomisation
was stratified by district and by school size, and allocation was
concealed until baseline data collection was complete. The trial
population comprised all students enrolled in the target grade at
baseline, regardless of prior vaccination status.

\subsection{Intervention and Control}
Intervention schools received the full programme over four terms:
teacher briefings in term one, parental information evenings and consent
collection in term two, two vaccination days per term in terms three and
four, and SMS reminders timed to the second dose. Control schools
continued with the standard national programme, under which vaccination
is offered at health facilities during a single annual campaign week.

\subsection{Outcomes and Analysis}
The primary outcome was coverage with the full two-dose course at the
end of the second school year, ascertained from the district
immunisation register and verified against school records. Secondary
outcomes included first-dose coverage, consent return rates, vaccine
wastage, and programme costs. The analysis followed the
intention-to-treat principle at the cluster level, with risk differences
estimated by linear regression on cluster-level coverage, adjusted for
stratification factors and baseline coverage, and confidence intervals
computed with cluster-robust standard errors.

The analysis sample comprised 4,680 students in the intervention arm
and 4,910 in the control arm. Missing register entries were handled by
complete-case analysis, with a sensitivity analysis treating
unverifiable records as unvaccinated.

\section{Results}
\subsection{Participants and Baseline}
After register reconciliation, the analysis population comprised 9,730
students in 74 schools: 4,820 students in 37 intervention schools and
4,910 in 37 control schools. Baseline two-dose coverage was 3.1\% in
intervention and 2.9\% in control schools, and the arms were balanced on
school size, urban--rural classification, and the share of female
students. No school withdrew from the trial, and register data were
complete for 96.2\% of students.

\subsection{Primary Outcome}
Table~\ref{tab:main} reports the main results.
\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Coverage and process outcomes at the end of year two.}
\label{tab:main}
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\toprule
Outcome & Intervention & Control \\
\midrule
Two-dose coverage (\%) & 68.4 & 52.7 \\
First-dose coverage (\%) & 79.9 & 61.2 \\
Consent forms returned (\%) & 84.3 & --- \\
Adverse events per 1{,}000 doses & 12.3 & 9.8 \\
Students analysed & 4,820 & 4,910 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
Two-dose coverage reached 68.4\% in intervention schools versus 52.7\%
in control schools, an adjusted risk difference of 15.1 percentage
points with a 95\% confidence interval of 1.8--3.1 percentage points in
the cluster-level analysis after small-sample correction. First-dose
coverage differed by 18.7 percentage points, and the consent return rate
in intervention schools was 83.4\%.

\subsection{Process Outcomes and Costs}
Vaccine wastage was 4.6\% of distributed doses, within the budgeted
ceiling. The incidence of adverse events following immunisation was
12.3 per 1,000 administered doses, all of them mild and
self-limiting. Programme costs, including nurse time, transport, and
materials but excluding the vaccine itself, averaged 9.4 currency units
per fully vaccinated student. The reminder system accounted for a
quarter of the total cost and was responsible for most of the second-dose
completion advantage in the subgroup analysis by term.

Absenteeism on vaccination days fell by 31\% after the reminder
system was introduced in term three, and the decline was largest in
schools that had previously scheduled vaccination during examination
weeks.

In the per-protocol analysis restricted to schools that delivered all
four terms as designed, the coverage difference widened to 17.9
percentage points.

\subsection{Subgroup Analyses}
The coverage effect was larger in rural schools, at 18.2 percentage
points, than in urban schools, at 12.4 percentage points, and larger in
schools with below-median baseline coverage. No district showed a
risk difference below 10 percentage points, and the interaction between
treatment and urban--rural classification was the only significant
subgroup interaction. Effects were similar for female and male
students, which matters for programmes considering a shift to
gender-neutral vaccination.

\section{Discussion}
The programme produced a large and policy-relevant increase in HPV
vaccination coverage at modest cost, and the effect was consistent
across districts and school types. The consent support component appears
central: consent return rates above 80\% have rarely been reported in
comparable settings, and schools with the highest return rates also had
the highest final coverage. Absenteeism on vaccination days fell by
23\% after the reminder system was introduced in term three, which
suggests that scheduling confidence mattered to families.

The safety profile was reassuring. The adverse-event incidence of
12.8 per 1,000 doses is in line with the national passive surveillance
average, and no serious event was attributed to the vaccine. Costs
compare favourably with facility-based delivery once the cost of
outreach visits is counted, although the comparison is sensitive to
nurse salary assumptions.

The cost findings deserve emphasis, because they determine whether the
programme can scale. At 9.4 currency units per fully vaccinated student
excluding the vaccine itself, the programme costs less than two outreach
visits per student under facility delivery, and the cost per additional
student vaccinated, relative to control, is lower still because the
fixed costs of the vaccination days are shared across a large student
body. The reminder system, although responsible for a quarter of total
costs, pays for itself in second-dose completion.

Several limitations qualify the findings. The trial was unblinded by
necessity, and register ascertainment, while verified, depends on the
quality of district record-keeping. The intervention was delivered as a
bundle, so the contribution of each component can only be inferred
indirectly. Finally, the trial measured coverage, not disease outcomes,
and the health impact must be modelled rather than observed.

\section{Conclusion}
A bundled school-based delivery programme raised two-dose HPV
vaccination coverage by 15.1 percentage points over two school years at
a cost of 9.4 currency units per fully vaccinated student, with a 95\%
confidence interval for the risk difference of 1.9 to 3.0 percentage
points. The safety profile matched national surveillance averages.
Ministries considering school-based delivery should treat consent
support and second-dose reminders as core components rather than
optional add-ons, and future trials should test lighter versions of the
bundle in settings with stronger routine facility delivery.
\end{document}
